Ways ‘negative emissions’ could slow 
climate change
The Paris Agreement, adopted at the COP21 sets out a global 
aim to limit average global surface temperatures to 1.5 0C
To get to net-zero emissions, we need “negative emissions”
technologies (NETs), or things which will suck the CO2 out of the
air to compensate for the ongoing release.”
1. Afforestation and reforestation
A/R-sequester CO2 at a rate of 3.7 tonnes/ ha/ year, and 
comes with an associated cost of $20-100 per tonne
Obstacles???

2. Biochar
The potential to sequester up to 4.8bn tonnes of CO2 per year
- Advantages / Disadvantages?
Biochar is generally produced through pyrolysis, a process that involves heating renewable biomass at high temperature
in an oxygen-limited environment. In the absence of pyrolysis, the biomass would either be burned in the open air or left
to decompose, resulting in much higher GHG emissions than those occurring during the production of biochar. In
addition, biochar is a stable form of carbon which can be stored in the soil and improve its fertility.

NZT Project
Carbon captured by Net Zero Teeside
will be buried beneath the North Sea
Net Zero Teesside aims to sequester
carbon emissions under the sea
NZT aims to capture CO2 produced in industrial processes and
power plants and transport these emissions by pipeline to offshore
storage sites several km beneath the North Sea
The aim, as the NZT project's name suggests, will be to reduce
carbon emissions in a number of carbon-intensive industries in the
North East to zero by as early as 2030.
